common_name: Flordabest Peach (Early Large-Fruited University of Florida Low-Chill Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; developed for about 250 chill units, well matched to zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Developed by the University of Florida for about 250 chill units, Flordabest is well matched to zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and peninsular Florida. It ripens very early, about a week to ten days ahead of TropicBeauty, with large, firm yellow melting flesh under 90-100 percent bright red skin. Trees are self-fertile, moderately vigorous, and semi-upright, setting heavy annual crops that need early thinning to size the fruit well. A strong pick for gardeners who want an early low-chill peach with above-average fruit size.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties
UF/IFAS Horticultural Sciences Department Stone Fruit Program

common_name: UFSharp Peach (Firm Non-Melting-Flesh Low-Chill Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; released in 2006 with an estimated 325 chill unit requirement, suited to zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2006 with an estimated 325 chill unit requirement, UFSharp suits zone 8-9 gardens wanting a mid-to-late-season low-chill peach. Unusual among low-chill types, its flesh is firm and non-melting rather than melting, holding up well to handling, with 50-70 percent red blush over yellow-orange skin. Trees are vigorous, self-fertile, semi-spreading, and productive, ripening in late May in north-central Florida trials. The firmer texture makes it a useful option for growers who want a low-chill peach suited to fresh market handling or preserving.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

common_name: Sunbest Nectarine (Early Low-Chill University of Florida Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 225 chill hours, one of the few reliable nectarines for zone 8-9 winters.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Released by the University of Florida in 2001, Sunbest needs only about 225 chill hours, making it one of the few reliable nectarines for zone 8-9 winters across the Gulf South and north-central Florida. It ripens very early, typically by early May, several days ahead of the widely grown Sunraycer, with yellow melting semi-freestone flesh under 90-100 percent red-blushed skin. Trees are self-fertile and heavy-bearing, though like most low-chill nectarines they need close monitoring for bacterial and fungal leaf spot in humid climates.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular 1159 — Florida Peach and Nectarine Varieties

common_name: Gulfrose Plum (University of Florida Low-Chill Blood-Red Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs about 275 chill hours; plant with another low-chill Japanese plum such as Gulfbeauty for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam in full sun. A University of Florida Japanese plum release needing about 275 chill hours, Gulfrose extends the low-chill Gulf series into zone 8-10 gardens from the Florida Panhandle through the warmer Gulf Coast. It ripens roughly a week after its sibling Gulfblaze, with a fruit development period near 95 days, yielding round, semi-freestone fruit with dark reddish-purple skin and striking blood-red flesh. It was selected alongside Gulfbeauty and Gulfblaze for resistance to plum leaf scald and bacterial spot. Plant it with another low-chill Japanese plum such as Gulfbeauty for reliable cross-pollination.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular HS250 — Growing Plums in Florida

common_name: Gulfruby Plum (Earliest-Ripening University of Florida Low-Chill Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 225 chill hours, the earliest-ripening Gulf series plum; watch for bacterial canker in humid climates.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam in full sun. The earliest-ripening member of the University of Florida's Gulf series of low-chill Japanese plums, Gulfruby needs only about 225 chill hours and ripens seven to ten days ahead of Gulfblaze. Fruit develops full red skin color a few days before it is ready to pick, with the sweet, juicy character typical of the Gulf breeding line. It is more susceptible to bacterial canker than its Gulf series relatives, so growers in humid zone 8-10 climates should watch for cankers and defoliation and remove infected wood promptly.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular HS250 — Growing Plums in Florida
UF/IFAS Horticultural Sciences Department Stone Fruit Program

common_name: Gulfgold Plum (Very Low-Chill Yellow-Fleshed University of Florida Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring; needs only about 150-200 chill hours, among the lowest-chill plums in the Gulf series.

directions: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic sandy loam with good air drainage to reduce spring frost damage to blossoms. Requiring only about 150-200 chill hours, Gulfgold is among the lowest-chill plums in the University of Florida's Gulf series, suited to the mildest winters found in zone 8 through 10. Fruit ripens from late May to mid-June, with yellow skin that develops a red blush and sweet yellow flesh with a faint greenish tinge that clings lightly to a small pit when fully soft-ripe. Its susceptibility to certain fungal and bacterial problems means it benefits from the same disease-conscious pruning and spray program used for Gulfbeauty and Gulfblaze.
sources: UF/IFAS EDIS Circular HS250 — Growing Plums in Florida
